extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and researchers seeking an encyclopedic overview of Latin American literature
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic survey describing the history, major movements, genres, themes, notable authors, and characteristic styles of literature produced in Latin America. Useful as a reference for identifying defining features, periods, and representative works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Latin American literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Latin American literature consists of the oral and written literature of Latin America in several languages, particularly in Spanish, Portuguese, and the indigenous languages of Latin America.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines the scope of the field (oral and written traditions; multiple languages). Frames what counts as Latin American literature and notes a long, complex tradition stretching back centuries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Association with magical realism
rubrics_metrics.description: Latin American literature rose to particular prominence globally during the second half of the 20th century, largely due to the international success of the style known as magical realism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why Latin American literature is often associated with magical realism and the Boom, and cautions that the region's literature is not limited to this style (many prominent writers do not fit the label). Examples: Gabriel García Márquez and Cien años de soledad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oral and Pre-Columbian traditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-Columbian cultures are documented as primarily oral, although the Mayans and Aztecs produced elaborate codices; the Incas used Quipu; oral mythological and religious accounts (e.g., Popol Vuh) were sometimes recorded after European arrival.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes the importance of oral forms and indigenous record-keeping as foundational to Latin American literature; contemporary survivals of oral narrative (Quechua, Quiché) are part of the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colonial literature characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: From the moment Europeans encountered the New World, explorers and conquistadores produced written accounts and crónicas; written culture was often in the hands of the church, and colonial practices stimulated debate about the ethics of colonization and the status of indigenous peoples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies primary colonial genres (letters, crónicas) and voices (conquistadores, church writers, mestizos and natives such as El Inca Garcilaso de la Vega and Guaman Poma) and highlights thematic concerns (ethics of colonization).

rubrics_metrics.name: 19th-century foundational fictions and national identity
rubrics_metrics.description: The 19th century was a period of 'foundational fictions' — novels in the Romantic or Naturalist traditions that attempted to establish a sense of national identity and often focused on the role and rights of the indigenous or the dichotomy of 'civilization or barbarism'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as criterion for works that aimed to build national canons; examples include Facundo (Domingo Sarmiento), Martín Rivas, María, Os Sertões. Such works commonly become canonical and are taught in schools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gauchesque genre
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'gauchesque' is an Argentine genre of poetry centered around the lives of gauchos (e.g., Martín Fierro).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies a regional/genre-specific form tied to national identity and frontier life; useful for classifying 19th-century Argentine poetry and epic forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modernismo (late 19th century) characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Modernismo emerged as a poetic movement (founding text Azul by Rubén Darío) and represented the first truly Latin American poetry movement to influence culture outside the region.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes modernismo as aestheticist and sometimes anti-political, though some modernists (José Martí, Manuel González Prada, José Carlos Mariátegui) introduced social critique; indicates the movement's role in forging transnational Latin American literary connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indigenismo
rubrics_metrics.description: Indigenismo is a trend dedicated to representing indigenous culture and the injustices that such communities were undergoing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serves as a thematic/ideological criterion for works that center indigenous subjects and social critique; examples in the text include José María Arguedas and Rosario Castellanos; links back to earlier critique traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avant-garde and vanguard movements (early 20th century)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the 1920s and 1930s, movements such as Stridentism, los Contemporáneos, and various avant-garde trends influenced poetry and prose; the Mexican Revolution inspired committed social-realist novels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Helps classify works by formal experimentation and political engagement; connects regional historical events (e.g., Mexican Revolution) to literary output (Mariano Azuela's Los de abajo).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lo real maravilloso (precursor to magical realism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Alejo Carpentier coined the term 'lo real maravilloso' and, along with Juan Rulfo and Miguel Ángel Asturias, was a precursor of the Boom and its signature style of 'magic realism'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides an origin concept for certain kinds of fantastic-real blends in Latin American writing; useful when attributing lineage or influence toward later Boom works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prose poetry tradition
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a vibrant tradition of prose poetry in 20th century Latin America; the prose poem becomes a prevalent format for lyrical philosophical inquiry and sensual sentiments of the region's poets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Names prose-poem masters (Borges, Neruda, Paz, Pizarnik, Braschi, Rafael Cadenas) and marks prose poetry as an important formal mode to look for in evaluating 20th-century Latin American poetic innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Boom: experimental narration and global prominence
rubrics_metrics.description: After World War II, the 'Boom' (c.1960–1967) featured writers who crossed traditional boundaries, experimented with language, mixed different styles, and embraced non-linearity and experimental narration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the Boom's formal hallmarks (non-linear structures, experimentation), internationalization (translations, attention abroad), and influences (Faulkner, Joyce, Woolf). Examples: Rayuela (Cortázar), Cien años de soledad (García Márquez). Also notes that not all major authors fit the magical-realism label.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-Boom characteristics and reactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-Boom literature is sometimes characterized by irony and humor, a turn toward popular genres, and reactions against the caricature reducing Latin American literature to magical realism (e.g., McOndo).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for identifying later 20th-century and contemporary works that distance themselves from Boom aesthetics, favor urban or popular culture subjects, or employ parody/irony (Alberto Fuguet, Giannina Braschi, Roberto Bolaño).

rubrics_metrics.name: Testimonio and collaborative/subaltern texts
rubrics_metrics.description: Testimonio refers to texts produced in collaboration with subaltern subjects (e.g., Rigoberta Menchú).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marks a documentary/activist genre that prioritizes collective or testimonial voices and socio-political witness; helps evaluate works for authenticity, collaboration, and political purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contemporary genre diversity and popular/avant-garde spectrum
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporary Latin American literature is vibrant and varied, ranging from best-selling popular authors (Paulo Coelho, Isabel Allende) to avant-garde and critically acclaimed writers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicates that contemporary evaluation should account for a wide spectrum of registers, markets, and experimental practices; includes attention to chroniclers, testimonio, crime fiction, horror, speculative fiction, and electronic literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political and social themes as central criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Recurring thematic concerns include identity, resistance, human rights, the status of indigenous peoples, anti-imperialism, and responses to political turmoil (dictatorships, Dirty Wars).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing Latin American works, note the degree to which they engage historical/political contexts and social critique (e.g., Martí's anti-imperialism, works foreshadowing dictatorships).

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical recognition via prizes and critical lists
rubrics_metrics.description: Prestigious awards (Cervantes Prize, Nobel Prize, Neustadt Prize, Jerusalem Prize, Camões Prize, national prizes) mark prominence among Latin American authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists laureates and prize winners as a way to identify influential figures and durable works; awards are treated as indicators of global recognition and canonical status.
